newsitem.title: USA: Buick hopes new cars will lead to market share gains.
newsitem.headline: Buick hopes new cars will lead to market share gains.

text.p: Buick executives said Tuesday they expect two completely redesigned cars and sharper brand images will reverse a market share slide at the General Motors Corp. upscale car division.

Buick General Manager Edward Mertz said it will take until the end of the 1998 model year before the division reaches its 6 percent target share of the U.S. passenger market. Buick currently has about 5.3 percent of the car market.

"We won't have the volume there to begin with, but over the next two years we're pretty sure we can get there," Mertz told reporters following an introduction of the 1997 models at Oakland University.
Year-to-date sales at Buick, which has had trouble appealing to younger buyers, are down 5 percent from last year at 295,640 units. Sales for all of 1995 were down 13.7 percent to 471,819.
Buick will introduce more new products in the 1997 and 1998 model years than it has before, Mertz said.

Included in that is an all-new version of its flagship Park Avenue due in October, the first time the car has been completely overhauled in 12 years. With the mammoth Roadmaster discontinued, the Park Avenue and its Ultra version become the largest of the Buick cars available.
Prices for the new Park Avenue, which is larger than its predecessor and features a new body structure and chassis, start at $29,995, with the base Ultra starting at $34,995.

An all-new version of Buick's mid-size Century will be introduced in the first quarter of 1997. Buick is positioning the new Century as a "premium family car without a premium price." Pricing for the Century has not been released, but Anthony Derhake, brand manager for the car, promised it would be on the "south side of $20,000."
"I promise you, the Century will have a very competitive manufactures suggested retail price," he said.
It has been 15 years since the Century underwent a major redesign. The new car is conservatively styled and is larger and better-handling than its predecessor, Buick said.
Because the engine is so quiet, it now includes a device that prevents the driver from grinding the starter by turning the key while the motor is running.
Derhake believes the new Century has the potential to sell more units than the previous model. Sales strategy includes pushing for more retail sales and offering dealer discounts.
Overall, Buick wants to bring the age of its ownership base into the 40s from the 50- and 60-year-olds who most often buy its cars now, Mertz said.

Using a combination of quicker-paced advertising and more targeted marketing, he said the division will also try to do a better job of selling its cars to specific demographic groups -- something GM is doing across all of its model lines.
"You won't see an Oldsmobile and a Buick being virtually the same car as you did 10 years ago," said Mertz.

He declined to comment on industry reports that Buick will drop its entry level Skylark. Buick officials acknowledged Japanese automakers are stepping up competitive pressures by cutting prices. But Mertz said he believes Buick will compete well on size, ride, handling and quietness features.
